title: Bead Making & Simple Crafts
subtitle: Make strong, well-designed bead bracelets, necklaces and bead bags, price them properly in naira and sell them with confidence.
description: A practical, step-by-step course in beadwork for beginners. You learn bead types, stringing materials and tools, then make stretch bracelets, crimped necklaces, earrings and right-angle weave pieces such as bead bags. You finish with colour design, quality testing, costing, pricing and safe selling on WhatsApp and at markets.
outcomes: Choose beads, stringing materials and findings that suit each piece's weight and use
Finish stretch bracelets with a glued surgeon's knot and necklaces with secure two-step crimps
Weave right-angle weave and plan the bead count for a small bead bag
Design pieces with the colour wheel and a 60-30-10 colour balance
Inspect and test every piece against a written quality standard and describe materials honestly
Cost a piece in full, set retail and wholesale prices, and sell safely online and at markets
audience: Women who are new to beadwork, or self-taught, and want to make durable pieces to wear, gift or sell.
tools: Flush cutters, chain-nose pliers, round-nose pliers and crimping pliers
Beading needles, a bead mat or towel, bead stoppers and a tape measure
Glass and crystal-style beads, seed beads and spacers
Beading wire, elastic cord, braided beading thread, crimp tubes, covers, clasps and jump rings
Jewellery glue such as G-S Hypo Cement
A smartphone with WhatsApp Business for photos and selling
A notebook for pattern cards, costing and a sales book

modules.title: Materials, tools and a safe workspace
modules.overview: Before you make anything, you need to know what you are buying. This module explains bead types and sizes, the threads, wires and metal parts that hold jewellery together, and the small set of tools and safety habits that make beading easy, neat and safe.

lessons.title: Bead types, sizes and how beads are sold
objectives: Name the main bead materials and say what each is good for
Read bead sizes in millimetres and seed bead sizes such as 11/0
Work out how many beads you need for a given length
Buy beads sensibly by strand, pack or weight

blocks.text: Beadwork in Nigeria has a long history. Coral and stone beads have been worn by royalty and at traditional weddings for generations, and today bead necklaces, bracelets and bead bags are sold at every big market and all over WhatsApp and Instagram. To make pieces people will buy, start by understanding the beads themselves: what they are made of, how they are measured and how they are sold.

blocks.alt: A loop of round beads on a string
blocks.caption: A strand of round beads: the size, material and hole of each bead decide what you can make with it.

blocks.text: Most beginners start with **glass and faceted crystal-style beads**, because they look good, are easy to find and are not too expensive. Keep natural stone and coral for later, when you can tell real material from imitation and can afford mistakes.
How beads are measured

Most beads are measured in **millimetres (mm)** across the widest part. A 4 mm bead is about the size of a peppercorn, an 8 mm bead is about the size of a chickpea, and 12 mm and above are bold statement beads. Oval and tube beads are given two numbers, such as 6 x 9 mm (width x length).

**Seed beads** use a different system called the aught size, written like 11/0 (say "eleven aught"). The bigger the number, the smaller the bead. As a rough guide, 15/0 is about 1.5 mm, 11/0 about 2 mm, 8/0 about 3 mm and 6/0 about 4 mm. Sizes vary a little between makers, so buy the same brand when you need beads to match exactly.

blocks.title: Check the hole, not only the bead
blocks.text: Two beads of the same size can have very different holes. Before buying, check that your wire or thread can pass through twice, because crimps and many weaves need a second pass. Carry a short piece of your usual wire to the shop and test a bead.
How beads are sold

items: **By strand:** many round beads come on a strand of about 40 cm (16 inches). Count is roughly 400 divided by the bead size in mm: about 100 beads of 4 mm, 66 of 6 mm or 50 of 8 mm.
**By pack or bag:** acrylic and crystal-style beads are often sold in bags of 100, 500 or by weight.
**By weight or tube:** seed beads are sold in grams, tubes or hanks (bundles of strung strands).
**Single pieces:** focal beads, pendants and natural coral are often priced one by one.

blocks.title: From design to bead count
items: Choose finished length
Subtract clasp length
Divide by bead size
Add 10% spare
blocks.caption: A simple calculation stops you running out of beads halfway through a piece.

blocks.title: Worked example: how many beads for a necklace
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kano wants an 18-inch (about 45 cm) princess-length necklace of 6 mm red glass beads with a lobster clasp.
steps: Finished length 45 cm is 450 mm.
The clasp, jump ring and crimps take about 2 cm (20 mm), so beads must fill about 430 mm.
430 mm divided by 6 mm per bead is about 72 beads.
Add about 10% spare for faulty or chipped beads: 72 + 7 = 79, so she plans for 80 beads.
One 40 cm strand of 6 mm beads holds about 66 beads, so she buys two strands.
blocks.result: She buys two strands, uses about 72 beads, and keeps the rest for matching earrings or a repair.

blocks.text: Buying beads well

Buy a few strands first and make one piece before buying in bulk. Look closely at each strand in daylight: are the beads the same size and colour, are the holes clean, is any coating already peeling? Coated beads (metallic or rainbow finishes) can rub off with sweat. Rub one firmly with your thumb before you buy a lot.

Be honest with yourself about stone and coral. Real coral and natural stones are costly. If a strand of "coral" is very cheap, it is probably dyed glass, plastic or reconstituted material. That is fine to use, but you must describe it honestly when you sell, which you will practise in Module 3.

takeaways: Glass and crystal-style beads are the best starting point for most beginners.
Beads are measured in mm; seed beads use aught sizes where a bigger number means a smaller bead.
A 40 cm strand holds roughly 400 divided by the bead size in mm.
Always add about 10% spare beads and test the hole size before buying.

activity.title: Make a bead reference card
steps: Collect at least five different beads you own or can buy cheaply (glass, crystal, acrylic, seed, wood).
Measure each with a ruler and write its size in mm, or its aught size for seed beads.
Tape or sew one of each onto a piece of card and label the material and size.
Calculate how many 8 mm beads you would need for a 20 cm bracelet, adding 10% spare.
activity.evidence: A photo of your labelled bead card and your bead-count calculation.

lessons.title: Stringing materials and findings: what holds jewellery together
objectives: Choose between beading wire, beading thread, elastic cord and memory wire
Read beading wire labels: strand count and diameter
Name the common findings: crimps, clasps, jump rings, pins and wire guardians
Match a stringing material to the weight and use of a piece

blocks.text: The beads are what customers see, but the **stringing material** and the small metal parts called **findings** are what decide whether a piece lasts a week or many years. Most broken beadwork fails at the string or the clasp, not at the beads. In this lesson you will learn what each material is for, so you choose on purpose rather than by guess.

blocks.name: spool-of-thread
blocks.caption: Thread, cord and wire are the hidden backbone of every beaded piece.

blocks.text: The four main stringing materials

head: Material
What it is
Best for
How you finish it
rows: Tiny steel wires twisted together and coated in nylon
Necklaces and bracelets with a clasp
Crimp beads or tubes with crimping pliers
Nylon thread or braided thread such as gel-spun polyethylene
Bead weaving, seed bead work, bead bags
Clear or coloured stretchy cord, about 0.5 to 1 mm
Surgeon's knot plus a dot of glue
Hard steel wire that keeps its round shape
Wrap bracelets and chokers that need no clasp
Small loop or end cap at each end

blocks.text: Reading a beading wire label

Beading wire is sold on spools with two key numbers. The **strand count** (often 7, 19 or 49) tells you how many tiny steel wires are inside. More strands make the wire softer, more flexible and less likely to kink, so a necklace drapes nicely. 49-strand wire costs more; 7-strand is cheaper and stiffer, fine for practice and simple bracelets.

The **diameter** is often written in inches, for example .015 or .019. Thin wire (about .010 to .013) fits small-holed beads such as pearls. Medium wire (about .015 to .019) suits most glass and crystal pieces. Thick wire (about .024) suits heavy stones and large beads. A good rule: use the thickest wire that will still pass through your beads twice.

blocks.title: Avoid ordinary sewing thread and old fishing line
blocks.text: Sewing thread frays and snaps under the weight of glass beads. Some makers use nylon fishing line for bead bags, but monofilament line can stiffen and weaken with age and sunlight. If you use it, buy a fresh, good-quality line and test your finished work by pulling firmly.
Findings you will use every day

items: **Crimp beads and crimp tubes:** small soft metal beads squeezed onto beading wire to hold a clasp in place. Tubes give a neater, stronger hold than round crimp beads.
**Crimp covers:** round shells closed over a finished crimp so it looks like a small metal bead.
**Clasps:** lobster clasps (strong, common), toggle clasps (easy to open, good for bracelets), magnetic clasps (easy but can open with a hard pull).
**Jump rings:** small open metal rings that join a clasp to chain or to a loop. Split rings look like tiny key rings and are more secure.
**Head pins and eye pins:** short wires used to hang beads for earrings and charms.
**Wire guardians:** small curved tubes that protect beading wire where it rubs against the clasp.
**Extender chain:** a short chain at the back of a necklace so one size fits more customers.
**Bead stoppers:** small spring clips that stop beads sliding off while you work.

blocks.title: Wire or elastic for a bracelet?
items: Beading wire with clasp
Elastic cord
blocks.caption: Choose wire for durable, premium pieces and elastic for quick, light, lower-priced bracelets.

blocks.text: Metal quality and finishes

Findings come in base metal (often plated brass, iron or zinc alloy), stainless steel, sterling silver and gold-filled. Cheap plated findings can turn dark or green with sweat. Stainless steel resists rust and tarnish and is a good middle choice. Some people react to **nickel** in cheap metals with itchy, red skin. Only call your findings "nickel-free" or "hypoallergenic" if the supplier states it in writing.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing materials for three pieces
blocks.context: For example, Blessing in Port Harcourt has three orders: a light seed bead anklet, a heavy agate necklace and a pearl bracelet for a bride.
steps: Seed bead anklet: light and flexible, so she uses 0.8 mm elastic cord with a surgeon's knot.
Agate necklace: heavy stones, so she uses 49-strand .019 beading wire, crimp tubes, wire guardians and a strong lobster clasp.
Pearl bracelet: pearls have tiny holes, so she uses thin .012 beading wire and checks that it passes through each pearl twice near the ends.
She chooses stainless steel findings for all three so they do not tarnish quickly.
blocks.result: Each piece has a stringing material matched to its weight, hole size and use, which reduces breakages and returns.

blocks.text: Start with a small kit: one spool of 19 or 49-strand .015 or .018 wire, a pack of 2 x 2 mm crimp tubes, crimp covers, lobster clasps, jump rings, a roll of 0.8 mm clear elastic, and a reel of strong beading thread. Check that your crimp size matches your wire; the wire packet usually lists the right crimp size.

takeaways: Most failures happen at the string or clasp, so choose them carefully.
More strands in beading wire means softer drape; diameter must suit the bead holes.
Use crimps for wire, knots for thread and elastic, loops for memory wire.
Describe metals honestly and only claim nickel-free if the supplier confirms it.

activity.title: Build your starter findings list
steps: Write down the three kinds of piece you most want to make first.
For each, choose a stringing material and a clasp or finishing method from this lesson.
List the findings you need and the quantity for ten pieces of each.
Visit a bead shop or check an online seller and note approximate prices beside each item.
activity.evidence: Your written starter findings list with materials matched to each piece and approximate prices.

lessons.title: Essential tools, standard sizes and a safe workspace
objectives: Identify the five core beading tools and what each is used for
Use standard necklace lengths and measure a bracelet size
Set up a clean, well-lit workspace that protects your eyes and posture
Apply safety rules for small parts, wire ends and children

blocks.text: You do not need many tools to begin, but you do need the right ones. Using kitchen scissors on wire or your teeth to flatten a crimp gives weak, ugly results and can hurt you. A few proper tools make your work neater from the first piece and last for years if you look after them.

blocks.name: toolbox
blocks.caption: A small, well-chosen toolbox matters more than a large collection of cheap tools.

blocks.text: The core tools

head: Tool
What it does
Tip
rows: Cut beading wire and head pins with a flat, neat end
Never use them on memory wire; it will dent the blades
Grip, bend, open and close jump rings
Choose smooth jaws so you do not scratch metal
Make loops on head pins and eye pins
Mark a spot on the jaw with a marker so loops come out the same size
Fold crimp tubes into a strong, neat shape
Match the plier size to your crimp size
Beading needles and a bead mat
Needles carry thread through beads; the mat stops beads rolling
A folded towel works as a mat to start

blocks.text: Also useful: a ruler or tape measure in centimetres and inches, bead stoppers, small containers with lids (empty, clean medicine or sweet tins are fine), a pair of small scissors for thread, jewellery glue such as G-S Hypo Cement for knots, and **memory wire shears** if you use memory wire.
Standard necklace lengths

head: Name
Approximate length
Where it sits
rows: Around the base of the neck
Just below the collarbone; the most popular length
Middle of the chest; can be doubled

blocks.text: For bracelets, measure the wrist snugly with a tape just above the wrist bone, then add about 1.5 to 2.5 cm so it moves comfortably. Large beads take up space on the inside of the bracelet, so add a little more for beads of 10 mm and above. Write sizes down for every customer.

blocks.title: Workspace check before you start
items: Bright light on the work
Bead mat laid out
Tools within reach
Children and drinks away
Glasses for wire cutting
blocks.caption: Run through this quick check each time you sit down to bead.

blocks.text: Look after your eyes and back

Beading is close, detailed work. Sit at a table, not on the floor or bed, with your elbows supported and your work at a comfortable height. Use daylight from a window or a white LED lamp so colours look true. Eye doctors often recommend the 20-20-20 habit for close work: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. Stand up and stretch every hour.

blocks.title: Small parts and children
blocks.text: Beads, crimps and jump rings are choking hazards. Keep containers closed and out of reach of young children, sweep the floor after work, and never let a small child play with loose beads. Do not make bead necklaces for babies or toddlers: the US Food and Drug Administration has warned that teething necklaces can cause choking and strangulation.

blocks.title: Wire ends and glue
blocks.text: Cut wire pointing down into a bag or your palm, because short ends can fly off. Wear ordinary glasses or safety glasses when cutting. Use glue in a ventilated space with the cap on between uses, and keep it away from children.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting up in a small space
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka shares a one-room apartment in Lagos with her husband and two children, aged 3 and 7.
steps: She buys a plastic box with a tight lid to hold all beads, findings and tools.
She uses the dining table after the children sleep, laying a dark towel as a bead mat so dropped beads do not bounce.
She places a rechargeable LED lamp to her left (she is right-handed) so her hand does not shadow the work.
When she finishes, she counts tools back into the box, runs her palm over the towel for loose beads and sweeps the floor around the table.
blocks.result: She works safely in a shared room, loses fewer beads, and the 3-year-old never finds loose parts.

blocks.text: Buy the best pliers you can afford, even if you start with cheaper beads. A decent pair of flush cutters and crimping pliers makes the difference between crimps that hold and crimps that slip. Wipe tools dry after use and store them in a pouch so the jaws do not get knocked or rusty.

takeaways: Five core tools: flush cutters, chain-nose, round-nose, crimping pliers and needles with a mat.
Princess length (43 to 48 cm) is the most popular necklace length.
Add 1.5 to 2.5 cm to the wrist measurement for a bracelet.
Keep small parts away from children and never make bead necklaces for babies.

activity.title: Set up and size
steps: Gather your tools and set up a workspace using the checklist in this lesson.
Measure your own wrist and the wrists of two other adults and calculate their bracelet sizes.
Use a piece of string to mark princess and matinee lengths on yourself and note which you prefer.
Take a photo of your workspace with tools laid out and labelled.
activity.evidence: A labelled photo of your workspace and a size note for three wrists.

quiz.q: Ada wants seed beads smaller than her 8/0 beads. Which size should she buy?
quiz.explain: In the aught system a bigger number means a smaller bead, so 11/0 (about 2 mm) is smaller than 8/0 (about 3 mm).

quiz.q: Roughly how many 8 mm beads are on a standard 40 cm strand?
quiz.explain: Divide about 400 mm by the bead size: 400 / 8 = 50 beads.

quiz.q: Which stringing material is best for a heavy stone necklace with a lobster clasp?
options: Thick multi-strand beading wire with crimps
quiz.explain: Heavy beads need strong beading wire (around .019 to .024) finished with crimps, ideally with wire guardians at the clasp.

quiz.q: A customer's wrist measures 16 cm. What is a sensible length for a beaded bracelet with medium beads?
quiz.explain: Add about 1.5 to 2.5 cm to the wrist measurement for comfort, giving about 17.5 to 18.5 cm.

quiz.q: Why should you not cut memory wire with ordinary flush cutters?
options: It is hardened steel and will damage the cutter blades
quiz.explain: Memory wire is hardened steel, so it dents and ruins ordinary flush cutters. Use memory wire shears or heavy-duty cutters instead.

quiz.q: Ngozi works at home with a toddler. Which habit best reduces the choking risk?
options: Keep beads in a lidded box and sweep the floor after each session
Tell the toddler not to touch
quiz.explain: Closed storage plus checking the work area and floor after each session keeps small parts away from young children.

modules.title: Guided practice: bracelets, necklaces and bead bags
modules.overview: Now you make real pieces, step by step. You start with a stretch bracelet and a secure knot, move on to a crimped necklace with a clasp and matching earrings, and finish with right-angle weave, the stitch used for many Nigerian bead bags, plus how to fix common faults.

lessons.title: Your first stretch bracelet and the surgeon's knot
objectives: Prepare and pre-stretch elastic cord correctly
Tie and glue a surgeon's knot that does not slip
Hide the knot inside a bead for a clean finish
Size a stretch bracelet for a specific wrist

blocks.text: A stretch bracelet is the best first project. It needs no clasp, uses few tools, and teaches the most important lesson in beadwork: **the finish decides the quality**. Most homemade stretch bracelets break because the cord was not pre-stretched, the knot was wrong, or the knot sat against a sharp bead edge. You will avoid all three.

blocks.name: knot
blocks.caption: A properly tied and glued surgeon's knot is the heart of a stretch bracelet that lasts.

blocks.text: What you need

items: Clear or coloured elastic cord, 0.7 to 1 mm thick (thicker for heavier beads)
About 22 beads of 8 mm for an average adult bracelet, including one bead with a slightly larger hole to hide the knot
A bead stopper or a piece of tape
Small sharp scissors
Jewellery glue with a fine tip, such as G-S Hypo Cement
A tape measure

blocks.text: Step by step

items: Measure the wrist and add about 1.5 cm for an 8 mm bead bracelet. Write it down.
Cut about 30 cm of elastic so you have plenty of cord to hold when knotting.
Pre-stretch the cord: hold each end and pull firmly, a few times, along its whole length. This takes out the first stretch so the bracelet does not sag after a few days.
Clip a bead stopper or tape about 8 cm from one end.
Thread your beads in your planned pattern. Lay the strung beads around the tape measure to check the length.
Remove the stopper and tie the surgeon's knot (below). Pull each end firmly so the knot tightens and the beads sit close without gaps.
Put one small dot of glue on the knot and let it sit for a minute.
Slide the knot inside the large-hole bead next to it, if it fits, then trim the ends to about 3 mm. Leave the bracelet to dry flat for a few hours before wearing.

blocks.text: Tying the surgeon's knot

The surgeon's knot is like the first half of a reef knot with an extra wrap. Hold the left end in your left hand and the right end in your right. Cross the right end over the left and **wrap it through twice**. Pull both ends to tighten. Then cross left over right and wrap through **once**. Pull hard on both ends, and also pull the beads on each side apart a little to lock it. The double wrap grips the slippery elastic so the knot does not slide open.

blocks.title: Stretch bracelet finish
items: Pre-stretch cord
Right over left twice
Left over right once
Glue dot
Hide and trim
blocks.caption: Each step removes one common cause of a broken stretch bracelet.

blocks.title: Glue choice
blocks.text: Use a jewellery cement made for knots and use only a tiny amount. Many beaders avoid quick superglue on elastic because it can make the cord hard and brittle at the knot, which is where it then snaps.

blocks.title: Protect the cord from sharp holes
blocks.text: Faceted crystal and some metal beads have sharp hole edges that slowly cut elastic. Place a smooth bead or a small seed bead on either side of sharp beads, or double the cord by passing through twice.

blocks.title: Worked example: sizing and counting for a customer
blocks.context: For example, Funke in Ibadan gets an order for a stretch bracelet in 10 mm wooden beads. The customer's wrist measures 17 cm.
steps: Because 10 mm beads are large, she adds about 2 cm: 17 + 2 = 19 cm.
19 cm is 190 mm. 190 divided by 10 mm per bead is 19 beads.
She uses 1 mm elastic because wood beads have bigger holes and the bracelet will be pulled on and off often.
She pre-stretches the cord, strings 19 beads, tests the fit on her own wrist (16 cm) and finds it loose, which is right for the bigger wrist.
She ties the surgeon's knot, glues it, hides it in a bead and lets it dry overnight before delivery.
blocks.result: The bracelet fits the customer comfortably and the knot is invisible and secure.

blocks.text: Easy variations once the basics work

items: **Stacks:** make three thin bracelets in colours that go together and sell them as a set. Sets often sell better than single pieces.
**Name and letter bracelets:** use letter beads between seed beads; check spelling twice before tying the knot.
**Charm bracelets:** add one small charm on a jump ring between two beads, closing the ring tightly so it cannot slip off the cord.
**Men's bracelets:** wood, matte stone-look or black beads in 8 to 10 mm with 1 mm cord.

blocks.text: Wear your first bracelet for a full week, taking it on and off by rolling it over your hand rather than pulling it wide. Note any loosening or gaps. This is your first durability test, and you will build on it in Module 3.

takeaways: Pre-stretch elastic before stringing so the bracelet does not sag.
Surgeon's knot: right over left twice, left over right once, pull hard.
A tiny dot of jewellery cement, then hide the knot in a bead.
Protect elastic from sharp bead holes with smooth spacer beads.

activity.title: Make and test two stretch bracelets
steps: Make one bracelet without pre-stretching and one with pre-stretching, using the same beads.
Tie a surgeon's knot on both and glue them.
Wear or roll both on and off ten times each day for five days.
Measure each bracelet at the start and end and note any change in length or gaps.
activity.evidence: Photos of both bracelets on day 1 and day 5 with your length notes.

lessons.title: Crimped necklaces with a clasp, plus simple-loop earrings
objectives: Crimp beading wire to a clasp using the two-step crimping method
Leave the right amount of ease so a necklace drapes well
Add a crimp cover and an extender chain
Make a simple loop on a head pin for matching earrings

blocks.text: A necklace with a proper clasp looks and sells as a finished product. The key skill is **crimping**: squeezing a small metal tube onto beading wire so the wire cannot slip out. Done well, a crimp holds for years. Done badly, by flattening it with ordinary pliers, it can slide open and drop every bead on the floor.

blocks.name: jewelry
blocks.alt: A person with a necklace and jewellery
blocks.caption: A well-crimped clasp turns strung beads into a necklace you can sell with confidence.

blocks.text: What you need

items: Beading wire about 15 cm longer than the finished necklace
Beads for your design, laid out on a bead mat
2 crimp tubes and 2 crimp covers that match your wire size
A lobster clasp, a jump ring and about 5 cm of extender chain
Optional: 2 wire guardians
Crimping pliers, chain-nose pliers and flush cutters

blocks.text: Crimping step by step

items: Thread one crimp tube onto the wire, then a wire guardian if you use one, then the loop of the clasp.
Bring the short end of the wire back down through the crimp tube, so both wires lie side by side inside it. Leave a tail of about 3 cm.
Slide the crimp tube up until there is a small, loose loop of wire around the clasp. Do not pull it so tight that the clasp cannot move.

Place the tube in the **back notch** of the crimping pliers (the one with a dip, nearest the handle). Make sure the two wires are not crossed. Squeeze firmly. The tube now has a groove with one wire on each side.
Turn the tube a quarter turn and place it in the **front notch** (the round one). Squeeze to fold the tube in half along the groove, making a neat, firm shape.
Tug the wire and clasp hard. If anything moves, cut off and redo it with a new crimp.
String your beads over both the wire and the tail for the first few beads, then trim the tail close.

blocks.text: At the other end, string a second crimp tube, a wire guardian if used, and the jump ring with the extender chain. Pass the wire back through the crimp tube and a few beads. Before crimping, **hold the necklace up in a curve**. If the beads stand stiffly like a bangle, loosen slightly. A necklace needs a little ease, about the width of half a bead, so it drapes softly. Then crimp and trim.

To hide the crimp, place a crimp cover over it in the front notch of the crimping pliers and close it gently until it looks like a small round metal bead. Squeeze a little at a time, turning it, so it does not crack.

blocks.title: One crimp, start to finish
items: Thread crimp and clasp
Wire back through
Back notch: groove
Front notch: fold
Tug test
Cover
blocks.caption: The two notches do two different jobs: first separate the wires, then fold the tube.

blocks.text: Simple-loop earrings

items: Thread one or three beads onto a head pin.
With chain-nose pliers, bend the wire above the top bead to a right angle.
Cut the wire about 1 cm above the bend (a little less for small loops).
Grip the very end of the wire with round-nose pliers and roll your wrist towards you to curl it into a loop that closes neatly at the bend.
Open the loop of an ear wire sideways (twist, do not pull apart), slip on the bead drop and twist closed.

blocks.title: Open rings sideways
blocks.text: Always open jump rings and loops by twisting one side towards you and the other away. Pulling them open into a C shape weakens the metal and leaves a gap that catches hair and lets parts fall off.

blocks.title: Worked example: a matching aso-ebi set
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Abuja is asked for a gold and wine-coloured princess necklace with earrings to match a wedding aso-ebi.
steps: She plans a 45 cm necklace: 40 cm of beads plus clasp and a 5 cm extender for flexibility.
She cuts 60 cm of 49-strand .018 wire (45 cm plus 15 cm extra for handling).
She crimps the clasp end, strings 6 mm wine crystals with a gold spacer every fourth bead, and a 12 mm gold focal bead at the centre.
She checks the drape, crimps the second end to the jump ring and extender, and adds two crimp covers.
For earrings she puts one wine crystal, one spacer and one wine crystal on each head pin and makes simple loops.
blocks.result: A matching set with secure crimps, a flexible length and earrings that use the same beads, ready to photograph and deliver.

takeaways: Crimp in two steps: back notch to separate the wires, front notch to fold.
Leave a little ease so the necklace drapes instead of standing stiff.
Always tug-test each crimp and redo any that move.
Open jump rings and loops sideways, never by pulling apart.

activity.title: Crimp practice and a finished necklace
steps: Practise five crimps on scrap wire, tugging each one hard.
Cut open your two best and worst crimps and compare their shape.
Make one princess-length necklace with a lobster clasp, extender chain and crimp covers.
Make a pair of simple-loop earrings that match it.
activity.evidence: A photo of your practice crimps beside your finished necklace and earrings.

lessons.title: Bead bags with right-angle weave, and fixing common faults
objectives: Explain how right-angle weave builds a flexible beaded fabric
Weave a practice strip using the two-needle cross-weave method
Plan the bead count and materials for a small bead bag
Diagnose and fix common faults in beadwork

blocks.text: Bead bags and purses are popular for weddings, owambe parties and gifts, and they sell at higher prices than single strands. Many are made with **right-angle weave (RAW)**, a stitch where each unit is a small square of four beads and every bead sits at a right angle to its neighbours. The result is a flexible, net-like fabric that can be shaped into a bag, a box, a coaster or a napkin ring.

blocks.name: handbag
blocks.caption: A small beaded purse is built from hundreds of tiny four-bead squares joined together.

blocks.text: Materials for practice and for bags

items: For practice: 6 mm or 8 mm round or crystal-style beads in two colours, so you can see the pattern clearly
Strong line: many bag makers use clear nylon line or a braided beading thread; braided thread resists cutting by crystal edges
Two beading needles, or stiffen the two ends of the line with a dot of clear nail varnish
Scissors, a bead mat and a lighter-coloured cloth so you can see your stitches
For a bag: a lining fabric, a zip or clasp frame (optional), and a handle such as a beaded strap or chain

blocks.text: Two-needle cross-weave, step by step

items: Cut about 2 metres of line and put a needle on each end. Pick up 4 beads and slide them to the middle.
Pass the left needle through the 4th bead from the opposite direction, so the two ends cross inside it. Pull both ends firmly. You now have a square of four beads: your first unit.
On the right needle pick up 2 beads. On the left needle pick up 1 bead.
Pass the left needle through the second (outer) bead on the right needle, crossing again. Pull firmly. That is your second unit, sharing one bead with the first.
Repeat steps 3 and 4 until the strip is the width you want.
To start the next row, turn the work and use the side beads of the first row as the shared beads for each new unit, adding fewer beads each time because one or two sides already exist.

blocks.text: Keep the tension even: pull each cross firmly, but not so hard that the strip curls. If your units look like diamonds instead of squares, you are pulling unevenly between the two needles. Count every unit; writing your pattern in a grid on squared paper makes this much easier.
From strip to bag

A simple flat bag is two panels of RAW joined at the sides and bottom, or one long panel folded in half. Sides are joined by weaving through the edge beads of both panels with new connecting beads. A fabric lining stitched inside stops items falling through and makes the bag stronger. Finish with a strap: a beaded rope or a ready-made chain attached with jump rings.

blocks.title: What makes a bead bag last
items: Neat finish
Lining and strap
Even tension
Strong line
blocks.caption: Build from the bottom: strong line and even tension matter more than decoration on top.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a small evening purse
blocks.context: For example, Aisha in Kaduna wants to make a small purse about 16 cm wide and 12 cm tall from 6 mm crystal-style beads.
steps: In RAW with 6 mm beads, each unit measures roughly the length of one bead plus a little, so she makes a test square of 5 x 5 units and measures it: 3.5 cm.
One unit is therefore about 0.7 cm. For 16 cm she needs about 23 units wide; for two panels 12 cm tall, about 17 units high each.
She works out the beads from her test square: 5 x 5 units used 60 beads, so about 2.4 beads per unit.
Two panels of 23 x 17 units = 782 units x 2.4 is about 1,880 beads. She adds 10% and buys about 2,100 beads.
She buys braided thread, a lining fabric and a ready chain strap.
blocks.result: By making and measuring a test square first, she buys the right amount and knows the bag will come out close to 16 by 12 cm.

blocks.text: Fixing common faults

head: Fault
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Stretch bracelet sags after a week
Cord not pre-stretched or too thin
Wrong crimp size or flattened with chain-nose pliers
Cut off, use matching crimp and crimping pliers
Redo one end with a little slack
Low strand count or bent while working
Crystal edges cut the line, or thread too thin
Use braided thread, reinforce with a second pass
Practise steady, equal pulls; check squares as you go

takeaways: Right-angle weave builds a flexible fabric from four-bead squares.
Two-needle cross-weave: 4 beads to start, then 2 and 1 with a cross each time.
Always make and measure a test square before planning a bag.
Most faults trace back to wrong materials or uneven tension, and each has a clear fix.

activity.title: Weave a test square and a coaster
steps: Weave a strip of 10 RAW units in two colours.
Add rows until you have a 5 x 5 unit square and measure it in cm.
Count the beads used and calculate beads per unit.
Use that figure to plan the bead count for a 10 x 10 cm coaster, then make it.
activity.evidence: A photo of your test square with a ruler beside it, your calculation and the finished coaster.

quiz.q: Bisi's stretch bracelets loosen and show gaps after a few days. What is the most likely cause?
options: She did not pre-stretch the elastic
She hid the knot inside a bead
quiz.explain: Elastic stretches most in its first uses. Pre-stretching before stringing removes that first stretch so the bracelet keeps its size.

quiz.q: In two-step crimping, what does the back notch (the one with a dip) do?
options: Makes a groove that separates the two wires
quiz.explain: The back notch presses a groove into the tube, putting one wire on each side. The front notch then folds the tube along that groove.

quiz.q: A finished necklace stands stiff like a bangle. What should you do?
options: Redo one end, leaving a little ease before crimping
quiz.explain: Beads need a little slack, roughly half a bead's width, so the necklace can curve and drape softly.

quiz.q: How should you open a jump ring?
options: Twist the ends sideways, one towards you and one away
Pull the ends apart into a C shape
quiz.explain: Twisting sideways keeps the ring's round shape and strength, so it closes neatly without a gap.

quiz.q: Aisha's 5 x 5 RAW test square used 60 beads. About how many beads will a 10 x 20 unit panel need?
quiz.explain: 60 beads for 25 units is 2.4 beads per unit. A 10 x 20 panel is 200 units, and 200 x 2.4 = 480 beads.

quiz.q: Bead bag thread keeps snapping near crystal beads. What is the best fix?
options: Switch to braided beading thread and reinforce with a second pass
quiz.explain: Crystal hole edges can cut nylon. Braided thread resists cutting, and a second pass spreads the load.

modules.title: Design, quality and pricing
modules.overview: Good technique is not enough on its own: pieces must look good together, pass a quality check every time, and be priced so you actually make money. This module covers colour and design, a finishing and honesty standard, and a step-by-step costing method in naira.

lessons.title: Colour and design: making pieces that look planned
objectives: Use the colour wheel to choose monochromatic, analogous and complementary schemes
Apply a simple colour proportion rule to a design
Plan a repeat pattern, a focal point and symmetry
Design for a real customer occasion such as an aso-ebi set

blocks.text: Two necklaces can use the same beads and the same technique, yet one looks expensive and the other looks random. The difference is **design**: which colours you put together, in what amounts, and in what pattern. You do not need art school. A colour wheel and a few simple rules will lift your work quickly.

blocks.name: choose-color
blocks.alt: A woman choosing colours from a palette
blocks.caption: Choosing colours on purpose, before stringing, is what makes a piece look planned.

blocks.text: The colour wheel in two minutes

The colour wheel arranges colours in a circle: the three **primary** colours (red, yellow, blue), the **secondary** colours made by mixing two primaries (orange, green, purple), and the in-between **tertiary** colours such as red-orange or blue-green. Three more words help: **hue** is the colour itself, **value** is how light or dark it is, and **saturation** is how bright or dull it is.

head: Scheme
How to pick
Effect
Bead example
rows: One colour in light, medium and dark
Pale pink, rose and deep wine crystals
Two or three colours side by side on the wheel
Royal blue with orange or gold
One colour plus the two beside its opposite

blocks.text: Neutrals such as gold, silver, black, white, cream and brown are your friends. They sit between strong colours, give the eye a rest and make bright beads stand out. A gold spacer between every few coloured beads is a classic Nigerian party look for good reason.
How much of each colour

A helpful starting rule used by many designers is roughly **60-30-10**: about 60% of the beads in a main colour, 30% in a second colour and 10% in an accent. Equal amounts of two strong colours often fight each other. Count it out on your bead mat before stringing.

blocks.title: 60-30-10 colour balance
items: 10% accent
30% second colour
60% main colour
blocks.caption: A small accent draws the eye, while the main colour holds the design together.

blocks.text: Pattern, focal point and symmetry

items: **Repeat pattern:** a short sequence repeated along the strand, such as A-A-B-spacer. Write it down so you can make the same piece again.
**Focal point:** one larger or special bead or pendant at the centre front, where the eye lands first.
**Symmetry:** both sides of a necklace mirror each other from the centre. Lay out the centre first, then build out both sides at the same time.
**Graduation:** beads get gradually bigger towards the centre, which looks classic and flattering.
**Texture:** mixing shiny crystal with matte or metal beads adds interest even in one colour.

blocks.title: Check colour in daylight
blocks.text: Bead colours look different under a yellow bulb, a white LED and sunlight. Lay out your design near a window in daylight before stringing, and take a phone photo. If the photo looks muddy, the colours may be too close in value: add a lighter or darker bead.
Designing for the person and the occasion

Think about who will wear the piece and where. Office wear usually works best with smaller beads (4 to 6 mm), quieter colours and princess length, so it does not swing onto a keyboard. Party and wedding pieces can be bolder: larger focal beads, more sparkle and stronger contrast. Older customers often prefer lighter pieces that do not pull on the neck, so consider acrylic or smaller glass for long necklaces. Men's bracelets usually look best in matte, wood or dark stone-look beads with little sparkle.

Skin tone and clothing matter too. Bright, saturated colours such as gold, coral red, emerald and cobalt blue stand out beautifully on dark skin. When you design for an outfit, match one colour exactly and use the colour wheel to choose the others, rather than trying to match every colour in the fabric.

blocks.title: Worked example: designing for an aso-ebi fabric
blocks.context: For example, Yetunde in Abeokuta receives a fabric swatch in emerald green with small gold patterns for a family wedding. Eight women want matching necklaces and earrings.
steps: Main colour (60%): emerald green crystal beads, to match the fabric.
Second colour (30%): gold metallic spacers, picking up the gold in the fabric.
Accent (10%): a few deep red beads, red being opposite green on the wheel, to make the design pop.
Pattern: green, green, gold, green, green, gold, with one red bead every 6 cm and a large green focal bead at the centre.
She makes one sample, photographs it on the fabric in daylight and sends it on WhatsApp for approval before buying beads for all eight sets.
blocks.result: The bride's family approves the sample, and all eight sets match because the pattern was written down and repeated exactly.

blocks.text: Keep a simple design notebook: a photo of each piece, the bead sizes and colours, and the pattern written as letters. When a customer says "I want the one you made for my sister", you can make it again exactly.

takeaways: Monochromatic is calm, analogous is harmonious, complementary is bold.
Start with about 60% main colour, 30% second colour, 10% accent.
A clear focal point and symmetry make a necklace look planned.
Write down every pattern and check colours in daylight before stringing.

activity.title: Three colour schemes, one bead
steps: Choose one bead colour you own a lot of.
Lay out three short designs on your mat: monochromatic, analogous and complementary, each using that colour.
Apply the 60-30-10 rule to each and photograph them in daylight.
Ask two people which they prefer and why, and note their answers.
activity.evidence: A daylight photo of your three layouts with the pattern written under each and the feedback notes.

lessons.title: Quality finishing, testing and honest product claims
objectives: Inspect a finished piece against a quality checklist
Carry out tug, wear and drape tests before selling
Describe materials honestly and avoid misleading claims
Reduce risks such as choking, skin reactions and copying others' designs

blocks.text: A customer judges your work in two moments: when she first sees it, and three weeks later when she has worn it to church, to work and to a party. A quality standard protects both moments. It also protects your name, because in a WhatsApp world one broken necklace can be shared with fifty people.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person ticking items on a checklist
blocks.caption: A written checklist makes every piece meet the same standard, not just the ones you made carefully.

blocks.text: The finishing checklist

items: **Connections:** every crimp is folded, firm and covered; every knot is glued and hidden; every jump ring is fully closed with no gap.
**Ends:** no sharp wire tails that scratch skin; trimmed thread ends are short and tucked.
**Beads:** no chipped, cracked, scratched or peeling beads; pattern matches the plan with no mistakes.
**Fit and drape:** correct length for the order; necklace curves softly; bracelet rolls on without strain.
**Look:** symmetrical from the centre; clasp sits at the back; nothing twisted.
**Clean:** no glue marks, fingerprints or fluff; polished with a soft dry cloth.

blocks.title: Make, test, improve
items: Make piece
Inspect checklist
Tug and wear test
Record faults
Adjust technique
blocks.caption: Every fault you record and fix makes the next batch stronger.

blocks.text: Three simple tests

items: **Tug test:** hold the clasp in one hand and the beads near it in the other and pull firmly. Repeat at the other end. Nothing should move or slip.
**Drape test:** hold the necklace up by the clasp and let it hang, then lay it on a curved surface such as a rolled towel. It should curve smoothly with no stiff sections or gaps.
**Wear test:** for each new design or material, wear one piece yourself (or ask a friend to) for at least a week of normal life. Note any loosening, colour rub-off, tarnish or skin irritation.

blocks.title: Worked example: catching a problem before it reaches customers
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha makes 20 bracelets with new metallic-coated beads for a market day.
steps: She wears one bracelet herself for a week before market day, as her standard requires for new materials.
By day 5, the gold coating has rubbed off on the inside of three beads and her wrist skin is slightly marked.
She records the fault: 'Coated beads, supplier X, coating rubs off with sweat in under a week.'
She sells the remaining bracelets only as 'fashion pieces for occasional wear' at a lower price, and stops buying that bead.
She asks her supplier for a sturdier finish and tests the new sample before buying in bulk.
blocks.result: Instead of twenty unhappy customers, she has one honest product description and a better supplier.

blocks.text: Honest claims

Call materials what they are. Say "glass crystal beads", not "Swarovski", unless you bought genuine branded crystals with proof. Say "coral-style beads" or "imitation coral" unless you know the coral is real. Say "gold-tone" or "gold-plated", not "gold". Only say "nickel-free", "hypoallergenic" or "stainless steel" when the supplier confirms it in writing. Honest wording builds repeat customers and avoids disputes.

head: Instead of
Say
Why
rows: Real gold is a precious metal; customers expect it to be genuine
Unless you can confirm the material
Strung on strong 49-strand wire with secure crimps
Only state what you can back up

blocks.title: Children's and babies' jewellery
blocks.text: Small beads and parts are choking hazards. Do not make teething necklaces or bead jewellery for babies; the US FDA has warned of choking and strangulation risks. For older children, use large beads, stretch cord that breaks away rather than strong wire around the neck, and tell parents the piece is not for children under three.

Write your checklist on a card and keep it on your work table. Tick it for every piece, not only for orders that feel important. A consistent standard means your cheapest bracelet and your most expensive bead bag both carry your name with pride.

Storage is part of quality too. Keep finished pieces flat or hanging, in separate pouches or bags, so crystals do not scratch each other and chains do not tangle. Keep them away from damp, direct sunlight and perfume, which can dull coatings and tarnish plated metal.
Respecting other designers

Learning from tutorials and copying a technique such as right-angle weave is normal. Copying a specific designer's distinctive piece exactly and selling it as your own is not fair practice, and can harm your reputation. Use what you learn, then change colours, proportions and details until the design is yours.

takeaways: Check connections, ends, beads, fit, look and cleanliness on every piece.
Tug test, drape test, and a week-long wear test for new materials.
Name materials honestly: glass, gold-tone, coral-style, unless proven otherwise.
Never make bead jewellery for babies; label children's pieces clearly.

activity.title: Run your quality standard
steps: Write your own finishing checklist using this lesson, on one page.
Inspect three pieces you have made against it and mark every fault.
Tug and drape test each piece, and start a one-week wear test on one.
Rewrite the product description of one piece using honest, specific wording.
activity.evidence: Your completed checklist for three pieces, wear-test notes and one honest product description.

lessons.title: Costing and pricing your beadwork in naira
objectives: Calculate the exact material cost of a piece from bulk prices
Add labour, packaging and overheads to find full cost
Set retail and wholesale prices with a clear profit margin
Check your prices against the local market and adjust

blocks.text: Many beaders lose money without knowing it. They count the beads, forget the clasp, the wire, the pouch, the transport to the market and their own time, then charge what a friend says is fair. A simple costing method fixes this. All naira figures in this lesson are **approximate examples**; prices change often, so always use your own current receipts.

blocks.name: abacus
blocks.caption: Careful counting of every cost is what turns a hobby into a business.

blocks.text: Step 1: cost per unit of each material

You buy in bulk but use small amounts, so first work out the cost of **one** unit. Divide the price you paid by how many you got. A pack of 100 beads for 2,000 naira is 20 naira per bead. A 10-metre roll of wire for 3,000 naira is 300 naira per metre, or 3 naira per centimetre. Keep these unit costs in a notebook or a simple spreadsheet and update them when you restock.
Step 2: build the full cost

items: **Materials:** every bead, spacer, wire or cord, crimp, cover, clasp, jump ring and extender.
**Labour:** your time. Choose an hourly rate you think is fair locally and use it every time. Time yourself making the piece.
**Packaging:** pouch, box, card, sticker or label.

**Overheads:** costs that are not in one piece but are real: transport to buy materials, data for WhatsApp selling, tool replacement, broken beads. A simple method is to add a percentage, such as 10% of material cost.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing a crystal necklace (approximate prices)
blocks.context: For example, Kemi in Lagos makes a 45 cm necklace of 6 mm glass crystals with gold-tone spacers. All prices are approximate examples, not market quotes.
steps: Crystals: 66 beads from a pack of 100 for about 2,000 naira = 66 x 20 = about 1,320 naira.
Spacers: 16 from a pack of 100 for about 1,000 naira = 16 x 10 = about 160 naira.
Wire: 60 cm at about 3 naira per cm = about 180 naira.
Findings: 2 crimp tubes, 2 covers, clasp, jump ring and extender chain = about 400 naira.
Material total: 1,320 + 160 + 180 + 400 = about 2,060 naira.
Labour: 1 hour at her chosen rate of 1,000 naira per hour = 1,000 naira.
Packaging: organza pouch and card = about 250 naira.
Overheads: 10% of materials = about 206 naira.
Full cost: 2,060 + 1,000 + 250 + 206 = about 3,516 naira.
blocks.result: Her full cost is about 3,500 naira. Any price below that loses money, even if it feels like a sale.

blocks.text: Step 3: add profit and set prices

Profit is separate from your labour. Labour pays you for your time; profit lets the business grow, buy more stock and survive slow months. Many small makers add a profit margin of 30% to 50% on top of full cost for retail. For Kemi, full cost of about 3,516 plus 40% profit (about 1,406) gives about 4,922 naira, which she rounds to **5,000 naira retail**.

A **wholesale price** is for people who buy several pieces to resell, such as a boutique or a reseller on Instagram. It must still be above your full cost, but leaves room for their profit. Kemi might set wholesale at full cost plus 15% to 20%, about 4,000 to 4,200 naira, with a minimum order of five pieces. Never sell wholesale below full cost.

blocks.title: What a retail price is made of
items: Profit
Overheads
Packaging
Labour
Materials
blocks.caption: Materials are only the base; a fair price covers every layer above it.

blocks.text: Step 4: check the market

Now compare. Look at similar pieces at your local market, on Instagram and in WhatsApp status updates from other sellers. If your price is far above theirs, ask why: are your materials better, is your finish stronger, or are you slower? You can buy materials in larger quantities, speed up with practice, simplify the design or target customers who value quality. If your price is far below, you may be underpricing your skill.

Review your prices every time you restock. If a pack of beads that cost 2,000 naira now costs 2,500, your unit cost per bead rises from 20 to 25 naira, and every piece using that bead costs more to make. Update your costing sheet first, then decide whether to raise the price, change the design or find a better supplier. Tell regular customers politely about price changes in advance.

blocks.title: Do not price from feelings
blocks.text: Lowering your price below full cost to win a customer means you pay to work. If a customer's budget is small, offer a simpler design with fewer or cheaper beads rather than the same piece at a loss.

takeaways: Always work from unit cost: price paid divided by quantity.
Full cost = materials + labour + packaging + overheads.
Profit is separate from labour; many makers add 30 to 50% for retail.
Wholesale must stay above full cost; check and adjust against the market.

activity.title: Cost and price two of your pieces
steps: Collect your receipts or current prices for the materials you use most and calculate unit costs.
Time yourself making one bracelet and one necklace.
Build a costing table for each piece: materials, labour, packaging, overheads, full cost.
Set retail and wholesale prices and compare them with three similar pieces you find locally or online.
activity.evidence: A costing sheet for two pieces with retail and wholesale prices and your market comparison notes.

quiz.q: Kike wants a calm, elegant necklace using only shades of blue. Which scheme is this?
quiz.explain: Monochromatic uses one colour in different lightness and darkness, which gives a calm, elegant look.

quiz.q: Using the 60-30-10 rule, how many accent beads should a 70-bead necklace have?
quiz.explain: 10% of 70 is 7. The main colour would be about 42 beads and the second colour about 21.

quiz.q: Which product description is honest and specific?
options: Gold-tone necklace with glass crystals on strong beading wire
quiz.explain: It names the materials accurately and states a real feature instead of a promise or an unproven brand.

quiz.q: A new bead's coating rubs off during a wear test. What should the maker do?
options: Sell them all quickly before anyone notices
Record the fault, describe remaining stock honestly and test a better supplier
Ignore it because it looked fine on day 1
quiz.explain: Recording faults and being honest protects customers and reputation, and testing a better supplier fixes the cause.

quiz.q: Materials 2,000 naira, labour 1,000, packaging 200, overheads 10% of materials. What is the full cost?
A customer wants Kemi's 5,000 naira necklace but has only 3,000 naira. Full cost is about 3,500. What is best?
options: Offer a simpler design that costs less to make
Sell it for 3,000 to win her
Use cheaper wire on the same design without telling her
quiz.explain: Selling below full cost loses money, and secretly lowering quality is dishonest. A simpler design meets her budget fairly.

modules.title: Your collection, selling and next steps
modules.overview: In this final module you produce a small, consistent collection, present and sell it safely on WhatsApp, Instagram and at markets, and plan your next 90 days. You finish with a portfolio that proves your skill and a clear path to your first regular customers.

lessons.title: Producing a small, consistent collection
objectives: Plan a mini collection of three to five related pieces
Batch-produce identical pieces using a written pattern card
Keep a production log with time, materials and faults
Document each piece with clear photos and notes

blocks.text: One beautiful piece shows you can bead. A small, consistent **collection** shows you can run a business: you can make the same design again, to the same standard, in a predictable time. This lesson turns your skills into a mini collection that becomes the heart of your capstone project.

blocks.name: creative-woman
blocks.alt: A woman working on a creative project
blocks.caption: A small, planned collection shows customers you can deliver the same quality every time.

blocks.text: Plan the collection

Choose a theme that links the pieces: a colour story (for example "Emerald and Gold"), an occasion (wedding guest, office wear, children's party favours for ages three and up) or a technique (stretch stacks). Then choose three to five items that work together, such as a necklace, a bracelet, earrings and a small RAW coaster or key holder. Pieces that can be bought as a set raise the average sale.
Write a pattern card for each design

items: Name and photo of the finished piece
Finished length or size and the stringing material with its size (for example 49-strand .018 wire)
Bead list with sizes, colours and exact counts
Pattern written as letters, from the centre out or clasp to clasp
Findings list and the finishing method
Time taken and full cost from your costing sheet

blocks.text: Batch production

Making several of the same piece at once is faster than making them one by one. Count out all beads for all pieces first into separate small bowls or lids, one per piece. Then do each stage across the whole batch: string all, crimp all first ends, crimp all second ends, add all covers. You stay in one rhythm, make fewer mistakes, and you notice at once if you are short of a bead.

blocks.title: Batch of five bracelets
items: Count beads into five lids
String all five
Knot and glue all
Dry overnight
Inspect and pack
blocks.caption: Doing each stage across the batch keeps quality even and saves time.

blocks.title: Worked example: timing one-by-one versus batch
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Enugu makes stretch bracelets for a school fundraising fair.
steps: Making one bracelet from start to finish takes her about 15 minutes, including finding beads and setting up.
Five one-by-one would take about 75 minutes.
In a batch, she spends 15 minutes counting beads for all five, 25 minutes stringing all five, and 15 minutes knotting and gluing all five: 55 minutes.
She saves about 20 minutes per five bracelets, about 4 minutes each.
She updates her costing sheet: labour per bracelet drops, so her profit rises at the same price.
blocks.result: Batching cuts her time per bracelet by about a quarter and makes all five identical.

blocks.text: Keep a production log

head: Date
Design
Qty
Time
Faults found
Fix
rows: One crimp slipped on tug test

blocks.text: The log shows where your time goes and which faults keep coming back. If the same fault appears three times, go back to the lesson for that technique and practise it on scrap before your next batch.

blocks.title: Photograph as you go
blocks.text: Take a quick photo of each stage: beads counted out, half-strung, finished. These process photos are useful for your capstone and also make good WhatsApp status posts that show customers your work is handmade.
Working with a helper

When orders grow, you may bring in a family member or a friend to help. A pattern card and your checklist make this possible: the helper counts out beads and strings, while you do the crimping and the final inspection until she is skilled. Pay helpers fairly and agree in advance how much per piece or per hour. Keep the final quality check as your own job, at least at first, so your standard stays the same.
Do not add a new design to the collection until the existing ones pass your checklist every time. A small range made well sells better than a large range with uneven quality.
Managing your stock

Keep beads sorted by colour and size in labelled containers, and write the date and price on each new bag. Before every batch, check the pattern card against your stock so you do not start a design you cannot finish. Keep a short 'low stock' list on your phone and buy those items on your next market trip. When a bead colour is discontinued or hard to find, note it on the pattern card along with a tested substitute.

Set aside a small 'repair kit' of spare beads from each design. When a customer comes back with a broken piece months later, you can repair it with matching beads. Free or low-cost repairs for genuine faults build loyal customers who tell their friends about you.

takeaways: A collection links three to five pieces by colour, occasion or technique.
A pattern card lets you remake any design exactly.
Batch production saves time and keeps pieces identical.
A production log shows recurring faults so you can fix them.

activity.title: Plan and start your mini collection
steps: Choose a theme and three to five pieces for your collection.
Write a pattern card for each design.
Make at least two pieces of one design as a batch, timing each stage.
Fill in your production log, including any faults and fixes.
activity.evidence: Pattern cards, a production log and photos of your first batch.

lessons.title: Presenting and selling: photos, WhatsApp, markets and safe payments
objectives: Take clear product photos with a phone and natural light
Set up a WhatsApp Business catalogue and write honest product posts
Package pieces attractively and handle custom orders with deposits
Protect yourself from fake payment alerts and other scams

blocks.text: You can make beautiful pieces and still sell nothing if nobody sees them clearly or trusts you. Selling is a skill like crimping: a few simple habits make a big difference. Most beginners in Nigeria start with people they know, WhatsApp, Instagram and local events, then grow from there.

blocks.name: product-photography
blocks.caption: A clear photo in natural light is often the first and only chance to win a customer online.

blocks.text: Phone photos that sell

items: Wipe the phone camera lens with a soft cloth.
Work near a window in daylight, out of direct harsh sun. Avoid the camera flash, which causes glare on crystals.
Use a plain background: white paper, a light cloth or a wooden board. Keep the background the same for your whole collection.
Take three photos per piece: the whole piece laid flat, a close-up of the beads and clasp to show quality, and the piece worn or on a stand to show size.
Tap the screen on the piece to focus. Keep the phone steady, resting your elbows on the table.
Crop and brighten slightly in your phone's photo editor, but do not change the colours. The customer must receive what she saw.

blocks.text: WhatsApp, Instagram and markets

items: **WhatsApp Business:** a free app separate from normal WhatsApp. Set up a business profile with your name, area and hours, and use the catalogue feature to list each piece with photos, price and description.
**Status updates:** post one or two pieces a day, process photos and customer feedback (with permission). Many sales come from status views.
**Instagram:** good for reaching people outside your circle. Use clear photos, the same background and short honest captions.
**Markets and events:** church bazaars, school fairs, weddings and owambe parties. Bring a mirror, a price list, a small card with your WhatsApp number and a few pieces at different prices.

blocks.title: Worked example: an honest product post
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Abuja posts her Emerald and Gold set on WhatsApp status and in her catalogue.
steps: Photo 1: necklace and earrings laid flat on white card. Photo 2: close-up of the clasp and crimp cover. Photo 3: necklace worn with a plain top.
Title: 'Emerald and Gold set: necklace and earrings'.
Description: 'Green glass crystals with gold-tone spacers. Necklace 45 cm with 5 cm extender, strung on strong beading wire with secure crimps. Matching drop earrings.'
Price: 'Set 7,500 naira. Necklace alone 5,000 naira.' (approximate example prices)
Delivery: 'Pickup in Wuse or delivery at buyer's cost. Ready in 2 days.'
blocks.result: The post answers the common questions (what, size, material, price, delivery) so buyers can decide quickly and trust what they will get.

blocks.title: Custom order flow
items: Agree design and price
Take deposit
Send sample photo
Balance paid
Deliver
blocks.caption: Clear steps for custom orders protect you from wasted materials and unpaid work.

blocks.text: Packaging and custom orders

Your pricing must already include packaging and the time you spend messaging customers. If you offer delivery, agree who pays and use a dispatch rider or courier you trust. Ask for the delivery fee upfront or include it in the price, and send the buyer a photo of the packed item before it leaves.

Simple packaging makes a piece feel like a gift: a small organza or cloth pouch, a card with your name and WhatsApp number, and a short care note ("Remove before bathing or swimming; store in the pouch; keep away from perfume"). For custom orders, write down the agreed design, size, colours, price and delivery date, and confirm it in a WhatsApp message. Many makers ask for a deposit, often around half, before buying materials, with the balance before delivery.

Reply to enquiries promptly and politely, even when the person does not buy. Many first-time enquirers come back weeks later for a gift or an occasion. When you deliver, ask happy customers if you may share their photo or words on your status. Real feedback from real customers is the strongest advertising you have, and it costs nothing.

blocks.title: Fake payment alerts and scams
blocks.text: Fake bank alert SMS messages and fake transfer screenshots are common. Never release goods because of an SMS or a screenshot. Open your own banking or wallet app (for example Opay, Moniepoint or your bank's app) and confirm the money is in your balance. Never share your PIN, password or one-time code with anyone, including people claiming to be from your bank.

Accepting transfers to a business account, or using a payment link from a provider such as Paystack once your business grows, makes records easier. Keep a simple sales book: date, customer first name, item, price, how paid and delivered. This feeds straight into your 90-day plan.

takeaways: Three photos per piece in daylight on a plain background: whole, close-up, worn.
Use WhatsApp Business catalogue and status, plus markets and events.
Write posts that answer what, size, material, price and delivery.
Take deposits for custom orders and confirm payments in your own app, never by SMS or screenshot.

lessons.title: Portfolio, certification evidence and your 90-day plan
objectives: Assemble a portfolio that proves your skill and quality testing
Track simple business numbers each week
Write a realistic 90-day plan with weekly targets
Choose your next techniques and growth steps

blocks.text: You now have the skills of a capable beginner beader: you understand materials, can finish stretch bracelets and crimped necklaces securely, can weave right-angle weave, design with colour, test quality, price properly and sell safely. This last lesson pulls your evidence together and sets your direction for the next three months.

blocks.name: certificate
blocks.caption: Your certificate stands on real evidence: finished, tested pieces and honest records.

blocks.text: What goes in your portfolio

items: Photos of your first piece from Module 2 and your best recent piece, side by side, to show progress
Your mini collection: three photos per piece, pattern cards and costing sheets
Quality evidence: your finishing checklist, tug and drape test notes, and a wear-test record for at least one piece
Feedback from at least two people who wore your pieces, written in their words
Your production log and sales book pages, even if sales are small so far

blocks.text: Numbers to track each week

head: Number
How to get it
What it tells you
rows: Whether practice is speeding you up
Names appearing twice in sales book

blocks.title: Your 90 days
items: Weeks 1-4: stock and photos
Weeks 5-8: first sales
Weeks 9-12: review and grow
blocks.caption: Each month has one main focus so the plan stays realistic.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kano has 20,000 naira (approximate) for materials and about 10 hours a week to bead.
steps: Weeks 1 to 4: make a collection of 15 pieces in two colour stories, photograph them and set up her WhatsApp Business catalogue. Target: 15 pieces, all passing her checklist.
Weeks 5 to 8: post on status daily, take a table at one church bazaar and offer aso-ebi sets to two wedding families. Target: sell 10 pieces and take 2 custom orders.
Weeks 9 to 12: review her sales book. Restock the two best-selling designs, drop the slowest one, and learn one new technique.
Every Friday: update her weekly numbers and spend 30 minutes fixing any recurring fault on scrap materials.
She keeps aside money from each sale to restock materials before spending any profit.
blocks.result: A clear plan with weekly targets she can check, instead of a vague hope to 'sell more'.

blocks.text: Next techniques to learn

items: **Wrapped loops:** stronger than simple loops; used for quality earrings and bead links.
**Peyote and brick stitch:** seed bead stitches for flat bands, earrings and patterned pieces.
**Knotting between beads:** a knot between each bead, traditional for pearls, so beads do not rub and only one bead is lost if the strand breaks.
**Multi-strand necklaces:** several strands joined to a multi-strand clasp or cone, popular for traditional and bridal wear.
**3D bead bags and boxes:** shaping right-angle weave into structured forms.

blocks.text: Look back at the very first bracelet you made in this course. Put it next to your best recent piece and note three specific things you now do better, such as neater crimps, even tension or better colour balance. This honest comparison is strong evidence for your certificate.
Growing your income further

There are several realistic directions for a beader with a solid foundation. You can specialise in one strong product, such as aso-ebi sets or bead bags, and become known for it. You can sell wholesale to boutiques and resellers. You can teach others in short paid classes once your own technique is consistent. Or you can offer repair and restringing services, which bring in steady small jobs and new customers.

Choose one direction for your next 90 days rather than all at once. Test it, track your weekly numbers, and decide at the end of the period whether to continue, adjust or try another direction. This simple rhythm of plan, act, measure and decide is what turns a craft into a dependable income.

Keep learning from reputable sources: established bead supply companies publish free tutorials, and practising a new stitch on scrap beads for a few evenings costs very little. Join local or online beading groups to see what others make, ask questions and share your progress.

blocks.title: Formalising your business
blocks.text: When sales become regular, consider registering a business name with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), which can be done online, and opening a separate business bank account. Separating business money from household money makes your numbers honest and helps you grow.

Above all, keep your standard. Customers return to a maker whose pieces last, whose descriptions are honest and who delivers when she says she will. Your skill will keep growing with every batch, every fault you fix and every customer you listen to.

takeaways: Your portfolio proves skill with photos, tests, feedback and records.
Track pieces made, sales, time, faults, returns and repeat customers weekly.
A 90-day plan has one focus per month and weekly targets.
Keep restock money separate and consider CAC registration as sales grow.

quiz.q: Why does batch production usually save time?
options: You do each stage across all pieces in one rhythm, with beads counted out first
quiz.explain: Counting out beads first and doing each stage across the batch reduces setup time and mistakes, and keeps pieces identical.

quiz.q: What should a pattern card include?
options: Bead list with sizes and counts, the pattern, findings, finishing method, time and cost
quiz.explain: A full pattern card lets you or a helper remake the design exactly and price it correctly.

quiz.q: A buyer sends a transfer screenshot and asks you to release the necklace. What should you do?
options: Check your own banking or wallet app to confirm the money has arrived
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked. Only the balance in your own app confirms payment.

quiz.q: Which three photos best present a necklace online?
options: Whole piece flat, close-up of beads and clasp, and worn to show size
One with flash, two in the dark
quiz.explain: Together these show the whole design, the quality of finishing and the real size.

quiz.q: Your production log shows the same crimp fault three times this month. What is the best response?
options: Go back to the crimping lesson and practise on scrap before the next batch
Use more glue on the crimps
Hide the fault with crimp covers
quiz.explain: A recurring fault means the technique needs practice. Covers only hide a weak crimp; they do not fix it.

quiz.q: Which is a realistic 90-day plan target?
options: Make 15 checklist-passing pieces in weeks 1 to 4 and sell 10 in weeks 5 to 8
quiz.explain: Good targets are specific, measurable and tied to a time period, so you can check progress each week.

finalQuiz.q: Which seed bead is the largest?
finalQuiz.explain: In the aught system a smaller number means a bigger bead, so 6/0 (about 4 mm) is the largest here.

finalQuiz.q: Esther needs a 40 cm length of 4 mm beads. Roughly how many beads, including about 10% spare?
finalQuiz.explain: 400 mm divided by 4 mm is 100 beads; adding about 10% gives about 110.

finalQuiz.q: Why do more strands in beading wire (for example 49 instead of 7) matter?
options: The wire is softer, more flexible and kinks less, so necklaces drape better
finalQuiz.explain: More, finer strands make the wire more supple and resistant to kinking.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the correct surgeon's knot for elastic?
options: Left over right once, then right over left once
Right over left wrapped twice, then left over right once, pulled tight and glued
finalQuiz.explain: The extra wrap in the first half grips the slippery elastic; a dot of jewellery cement secures it.

finalQuiz.q: When crimping, what is the front (round) notch used for?
options: Folding the grooved tube in half into a neat, firm shape
finalQuiz.explain: The back notch separates the wires with a groove; the front notch folds the tube along that groove.

finalQuiz.q: In two-needle right-angle weave, after the first four-bead unit, what do you add for each new unit?
options: Two beads on one needle and one on the other, then cross through the outer bead
finalQuiz.explain: Each new unit shares one bead with the previous unit, so only three new beads are added before crossing.

finalQuiz.q: A fabric is royal blue. Which bead colour gives a complementary accent?
finalQuiz.explain: Orange sits opposite blue on the colour wheel, giving a bold complementary contrast; gold reads as a warm orange-yellow.

finalQuiz.q: Which wording is honest for a cheap red bead necklace of unknown material?
finalQuiz.explain: Unless you can confirm the material, describe the look, not a valuable material you cannot prove.

finalQuiz.q: A mother asks for a bead necklace for her 8-month-old baby. What should you do?
options: Politely decline and explain the choking and strangulation risk
Use strong wire so it cannot break
Make it but tell her to watch the baby
finalQuiz.explain: Bead necklaces for babies are a choking and strangulation hazard; the US FDA has warned against teething necklaces.

finalQuiz.q: Materials 1,800 naira, labour 1,200, packaging 300, overheads 180. With 40% profit on full cost, what is the retail price before rounding?
A buyer's SMS 'credit alert' arrives for a custom bead bag. What is the safe next step?
options: Confirm the money in your own banking or wallet app before releasing the bag
Ask the buyer for their PIN
finalQuiz.explain: SMS alerts can be faked. Only your own app balance confirms payment, and you never ask for or share PINs.

finalQuiz.q: Halima's sales book shows two designs selling well and one not selling at all after 8 weeks. What should her plan do next?
options: Make more of the slow design to push it
Restock the best sellers, drop or redesign the slow one, and keep tracking weekly
finalQuiz.explain: Weekly numbers show real demand; restocking winners and changing what does not sell uses limited money wisely.

capstone.title: Craft collection and quality portfolio
capstone.brief: Produce a mini collection of at least three related, quality-tested pieces (for example a crimped necklace, a stretch bracelet and a right-angle weave item such as a small bead bag, coaster or key holder) and submit a portfolio with pattern cards, test records, costing sheets, product photos, feedback and a 90-day plan.
steps: Choose a theme and plan three to five pieces using the colour wheel and the 60-30-10 rule.
Write a pattern card for each design with bead counts, materials and finishing method.
Make the pieces, including at least one batch of two identical pieces, and record a production log.
Inspect every piece with your finishing checklist, tug and drape test them, and wear-test at least one piece for a week.
Cost each piece in full and set retail and wholesale prices, checked against three similar pieces in your market.
Photograph each piece (whole, close-up, worn), write honest product descriptions and list them in a WhatsApp Business catalogue.
Collect feedback from at least two people and write a 90-day plan with monthly focus and weekly targets.
evidence: Photos of at least three finished pieces, three angles each
Production log with times, faults and fixes
Completed finishing checklist and tug, drape and wear-test notes
Costing sheets with full cost, retail and wholesale prices
Honest product descriptions or catalogue screenshots
Written feedback from at least two wearers
A photo of your first piece beside your best piece
